CR-D-76 is confirmed: a czar that can reach Tube but not its members keeps its lease forever, and its members can never depose it. It reproduces deterministically at escalation level 1 with no source changes, and the evidence is complete on the RMember channels and real HermesNode clients. Both the worktree and the newer source-root HEAD (aae88ecf, same czar.go) show it.

- **Source**: Code Review
- **Novelty**: NEW. I searched upstream glycerine/rpc25519 on 2026-11-23: 0 issues for "czar", 0 for "partition", and the repo has no PRs at all (open, closed or merged). Upstream's newest tube/czar.go commit is 42be7a1, the same as local, no local branch has a newer czar.go, and the persistent-findings lookup was empty.
- **Location**: tube/czar.go:1269
- **Severity**: Medium

## Description
The czar's renewal arm (tube/czar.go:1269-1309) re-CASes the czar key through Tube every 1 s. Its only failure exit is a CAS error. Nothing in the czar's loop (czar.go:1212-1345) checks whether any member has pinged it.

Members can only become czar by CASing that same key. Tube's `doCAS` rejects a CAS from anyone else while the current lease is valid. So a czar that reaches Tube but not its members is never replaced:
- Each member cycles forever: ping fails, state goes to unknown, its CAS is rejected, it pings again (czar.go:1390-1410, 1418-1434, 1471-1491).
- The czar's `expireSilentNodes` (czar.go:306-362) drops every member and tells the czar's own consumer that the membership is just the czar.
- The members' Hermes nodes lose their operating lease and refuse every Read/Write/RMW.

## Trigger scenario
1. A 3-node Tube cluster runs with 4 RMembers. Member 0 wins the czar key at epoch 1; members 1-3 ping it and hold operating leases.
2. An asymmetric network fault: members can no longer reach the czar's rpc server (the address they dial for `Czar.Ping`). The czar's outbound connections to Tube keep working, and members still reach Tube and each other.
3. Each member's ping fails and its CAS on the czar key is rejected ("rejected write … current leasor=<czar>"). It re-dials, the ping fails again, and its next CAS is rejected again because the czar renewed its 5 s lease less than 1 s earlier. This never ends.
4. After about 8 s the czar announces a membership of only itself, and it keeps renewing every 1 s.

## Developer intent
- czar.go:659-665: "If the Czar cannot be reached, the Hermes node starts trying to become the Czar … Repeat until either the current Czar can be reached or a new Czar is elected." Neither happened in 30 simulated minutes.
- The design notes at the end of czar.go name this outcome as one to avoid: "…So no new czar is elected / The system appears to have a valid czar that's actually dead (from the masters' perspective)". They also say an unreachable czar should cost only "an availability blip", and that when the czar fails "the next master to write to the czar key in Raft becomes the new czar".
- tube/CLAUDE.md: "If or when the czar fails, all other members of the hermes replicas will contend to be czar."
- No test, comment or commit accepts an indefinite group of just the czar.

## Reproduction result
I isolated only the czar's member-facing server node in the in-repo network simulator (`simnet.AlterCircuit(srv_<czar>, ISOLATE, wholeHost=false)`), then observed. Command: `repro/test_bugCR-D-76_czar_never_deposed.sh "" 3`, which runs `cd tube && go test -tags synctest -count=1 -v -run 'Test_CRD76_' .` and the same in `tube/hermes`. All 3 runs were identical:
```
CRD76 [t=+  21.5s] PHASE A (healthy): czar '..._0' state=AmCzar CzarLeaseEpoch=1 ... czar PeerNames=[..._1 ..._2 ..._3]
CRD76 [t=+  21.5s] topology(before fault): auto-cli-from-srv_..._0-to-srv_node_0___... -> srv_node_0
CRD76 [t=+  21.5s] topology(before fault): srv_..._0 -> ..._1_pinger_...
CRD76 [t=+  21.5s] FAULT injected: simnet.AlterCircuit('srv_..._0', ISOLATE, wholeHost=false) undo=UNISOLATE ...
CRD76 [t=+ 201.6s] PHASE B +180s: czar state=AmCzar epoch=1 leaseLeft=4.01s renewals(+150 since fault) czarPeerNames=[] | m1{state=NotCzar rejectedCAS(+26) leaseRenewals(+0) hasOperLease=false} ...
CRD76 [t=+ 201.6s]   czar's last membership upcall (to its own consumer) at +8.405s after fault: PeerNames=[] CallFrom='czar.go:1265 AmCzar: expireCheckCh changed'
CRD76 [t=+ 201.6s] BUG-CHECK: czar never deposed=true (stayed AmCzar=true, epoch unchanged=true, no member ever czar=true), czar kept renewing via Tube=true (150 renewals), czar membership shrank to only itself=true, all 3 members without operating lease=true
CRD76 [t=+ 231.6s] PHASE C: new czar member[1] epoch=2 PeerNames=[..._2 ..._3]
CRD76 [t=+ 231.6s] CONTROL: after the old czar is crash-stopped, members elect a new czar and regain operating leases = true
CRD76H [t=+  21.5s] PHASE A (healthy): replica[1] czarState=NotCzar HermesNode.Read(probe,-1) err=error key not found
CRD76H [t=+  36.5s] PHASE B + 15s: r0{AmCzar Read.err=error key not found} r1{NotCzar Read.err=error no valid operating membership lease} ...
CRD76H [t=+ 201.5s] HERMES-CHECK: czar still AmCzar=true; no member became czar=true; member Read samples gated by ErrNoOperatingLease=36/36; czar Read samples gated=0
```
A 30-minute window (`CRD76_OBSERVE_SEC=1800`) shows the same thing:
```
CRD76 [t=+1821.7s] PHASE B +1800s: czar state=AmCzar epoch=1 leaseLeft=4.776s renewals(+1501 since fault) czarPeerNames=[] | m1{state=NotCzar rejectedCAS(+279) leaseRenewals(+0) hasOperLease=false} ...
```
- **Heal control:** removing the fault lets the members rejoin the same czar (epoch 1, all 3 back). Expected behaviour, for contrast: the crash-stop control above, where a member becomes czar at epoch 2 within 30 s.
- **Test-harness limit:** the 30-minute run drains a test-only channel (`verifyPeerReplicaOrNot`, capacity 290, tube.go:4475-4479), the same way the cluster setup helper does. Without that, two runs hit `panicAtCap` at about 10 and 15 simulated minutes, after showing the same state up to that point.
- **Branch exercised:** the simulator never fails the member's dial, so the member exits hit were czar.go:1418-1434 and 1478-1491. Over real TCP a blocked port takes the cited czar.go:1390-1410 branch, which ends in the same rejected-CAS loop.

## Recommendation
Make czar-ship depend on whether members can reach the czar, not only on Tube:
- Have members that can't reach the czar but can reach Tube record that in Tube (for example a short-leased `members/<name>` or `czar-unreachable/<name>` key).
- In the renewal arm, have the czar skip renewing and step down when it sees such reports, or when no member has pinged it for longer than the member lease while Tube lists live members. A reachable member then wins the next CAS.
- Requiring Tube evidence of live members avoids flapping a czar that is genuinely alone.
- Keep the simulator test as a regression test.

## Checklist
1. **Level 0/1 alone?** Yes, level 1. Only the public `NewRMember`/`Start` API, consumers draining its channels, and the simulator's own network-fault hook were used. `Czar.State()` and `Czar.inspect()` were used read-only. No state injection and no source patch.
2. Not applicable (no level 2 or 3).
3. **Real consumer:** `HermesNode.Read` (tube/hermes/hermes.go:2645-2648) returned `ErrNoOperatingLease` in 36 of 36 member samples. It is gated by `hasOperatingLease()` (hermes.go:2694-2696), which only `OperatingLeaseRenewCh` refreshes (hermes.go:2811). On the czar, the membership upcall from czar.go:1265 carries `PeerNames=[]` into `applyMembershipChange` (hermes.go:2815).
4. **Permanent?** It lasts as long as the fault does: 30 simulated minutes, with nothing inside the system resolving or masking it. Only healing the network or killing the czar ends it.

# CR-D-77: The member's czar ping client dials with no connect timeout

I reproduced this with only public APIs and real faults. A member that needs to reach a dead or hung czar is stuck for about 135 s (dead host) or for as long as the czar stays hung (TLS). The designed failover takes about 5 s.

- **Source**: Code Review
- **Novelty**: NEW
- **Severity**: Medium
- **Location**: `tube/czar.go:1389` (the pinger is built at `tube/czar.go:1382-1389`; the unbounded dial is at `cli.go:184-199`)
- **Reproduction test**: `repro/test_bugCR-D-77_czar_dial_no_connect_timeout_test.go`, run by `repro/test_bugCR-D-77_czar_dial_no_connect_timeout.sh`. Escalation reached Level 0.
- **Persistent record**: `confirmation/CR-D-77/issue.json` passes `specular findings validate` (`"valid": true`). The full write-up is in `confirmation/CR-D-77/confirmation.md` and the Phase-1 evidence in `confirmation/CR-D-77/investigation.md`.

## Description
A member tries to take the czar key with a CAS. If another member holds an unexpired lease, the CAS is rejected and the member has to contact that czar. It copies its own rpc config, which has `ConnectTimeout` 0, and calls `rpc.NewClient(...).Start()` (`czar.go:1382-1389`).

`ConnectTimeout` 0 is the `rpc.NewConfig` default, documented at `cli.go:1143-1145` as "The default of 0 mean wait forever". Tube never sets it. The shipped `tube/cmd/{member,hermes}/example.cfg` don't set it either, and they use TLS. `Start()` is just `StartWithCtx(context.Background())`.

So `runClientMain` dials with a background context and a `net.Dialer` with no timeout (`cli.go:184-199`). Neither the TCP connect nor the TLS handshake has a time limit. The member's whole membership state machine runs on one goroutine, and it blocks there:
- about 135 s against a dead czar host, until the kernel gives up on SYN retries;
- indefinitely against a hung czar process under TLS.

The designed fail-fast path (`czar.go:1390-1411`: wait out the ≤5 s lease, then CAS for czar-ship) only runs after that delay.

## Trigger scenario
1. A real 3-replica Tube cluster runs on real sockets. Member `czarA`, a separate OS process, wins the CAS on `<tableSpace>/czar` (5 s lease, renewed every 1 s).
2. One of two faults hits `czarA`:
   - **Host dead**: all packets to and from its port are dropped with nftables in a private network namespace, and the process is SIGKILLed.
   - **Process hung**: the process gets SIGSTOP while its kernel stays alive.
3. While the lease is still valid, member `memberB` starts with `tube.NewRMember(ts, cfg).Start()`. Any member restart or `continue fullRestart` inside that ≤5 s window takes the same path. Its CAS is rejected, it moves to the NotCzar state, and it dials `czarA` at `czar.go:1387-1389`.
4. **Expected**: the dial fails, B waits out the lease (≤5 s), takes over as czar, and starts sending operating-lease renewals to hermes.
5. **Actual**: B stays blocked in `Start()`. While blocked it cannot take over, cannot renew its hermes operating lease, and does not respond to `Halt`.

## Developer intent
- **Failover is meant to be bounded by the lease.**
  - On a dial error, `czar.go:1390-1411` logs "could not contact czar ... might have to wait out the lease", sleeps out the remaining lease, then runs `continue fullRestart`.
  - The design note at `czar.go:2086` says "When the czar dies the whole process repeats".
  - `tube/CLAUDE.md:7` says "If or when the czar fails, all other members ... will contend to be czar".
- **Every other blocking step in this loop has a timeout:**
  - the CAS: comment "stuck here 35 minutes huh. use a timeout." (`czar.go:1032`);
  - the lease renewal: comment "hung here on cluster leader bounce" (`czar.go:1293`);
  - the Ping right after the dial, which uses a 5 s context (`czar.go:1418`).
- **The same problem was fixed at a different call site.** Commit 6afee204 says "add rpc.Client.StartWithCtx to avoid hung state in Client.Start for autocli from srv.go:2333". Commit 115dd94c gives autoclients a `ConnectTimeout`. The czar pinger was not changed.
- **"0 means wait forever" is not a deliberate no-timeout policy for connects.** It is an opt-in knob. Commit 2e9cb553 ("more timeout elimination") removed read and write timeouts because cutting a message in half is unrecoverable; that argument doesn't apply to connecting.
- **Existing tests don't cover this.** The czar tests (808/809) run only under the simulated network, which never takes this dial path.
- **No prior report exists.**
  - The GitHub tracker for glycerine/rpc25519 has 0 issues and 0 PRs in any state. Searches for czar, ConnectTimeout, dial, hermes, timeout and hang return nothing.
  - Upstream master HEAD (150bf57a) is this tree's base. The latest upstream commits touching `czar.go` and `cli.go` are already in this tree, so no fix has landed.
  - The persistent-findings lookup is empty.

## Reproduction result
Command: `timeout 15m repro/test_bugCR-D-77_czar_dial_no_connect_timeout.sh`. It builds the test binary from the unmodified worktree and runs it inside `unshare -rn`. Exit code 0; all four variants pass. Full log is in `repro/CR-D-77.log`, summary in `repro/CR-D-77.run.out`.

    goroutine 1769 [IO wait]: crypto/tls.(*Conn).readHandshake / clientHandshake / handshakeContext / crypto/tls.dial tls.go:172 / tls.(*Dialer).DialContext / rpc25519.(*Client).runClientMain cli.go:199
```
What this shows:
- **Stuck at the cited code.** In V1 and V2 the member dialed within 0.17–0.18 s of the fault. It then stayed stuck at `czar.go:1389` → `cli.go:199` while the czar key's lease had already expired. No member held czar-ship, and a CAS would have won.
- **The cause is the missing time limit.** V0 (the dial fails at once) and V3 (TCP only, where the following 5 s Ping applies) both fail over in about 5–6 s. The only difference from V1/V2 is whether the dial is bounded.
- **The 135 s figure.** The finding estimated about 127 s; this kernel (6.18, `tcp_syn_retries=6`) gave up after about 135 s.
- **Run history.** One earlier full run passed all four variants. Another was killed partway through V2 by an unrelated job on the host that kills generic `tube.test` binaries; after renaming the test binary, the run above is clean.

### Checklist
1. **Did Level 0 or Level 1 alone trigger it? Yes, Level 0.**
   - Only public entry points were used (`SetupTestClusterWithCustomConfig` and `tube.NewRMember(...).Start()`), on real TLS sockets.
   - The faults are the ones the finding names: SIGKILL or SIGSTOP of the czar's process, plus an nftables packet drop on its port in a private namespace to model a dead host.
   - Nothing was changed in the source (worktree `git diff` is empty) and no state or failpoints were injected.
   - The only timing choice is starting the member within the 5 s lease window, which is a natural ordering of events.
2. **Level 2 or 3 used?** No, so no injected precondition needs justifying.
3. **Real consumer that sees a wrong outcome.** These are the outputs of the membership API that hermes consumes; each was observed through that same API:
   - **Czar-ship**: `czar.go:779-783` ("Start elects a Czar") — it stayed vacant for about 130 s in V1 and indefinitely in V2.
   - **Operating lease**: `OperatingLeaseRenewCh`, wired into hermes at `tube/hermes/hermes.go:2724-2725` and read at `:2811` — no renewals arrived during the stall. Hermes ignores INV/VALIDATE/ACK messages without a lease (`hermes.go:2694-2696`, `:2820-2850`); that last step is argued from the code.
   - **Shutdown**: `hermes.RunFromDiskConfig` (`hermes.go:2731-2735`) calls `RequestStop()` and then waits on `Halt.Done`. That wait did not complete in V2.
4. **Permanent, or later fixed or hidden?**
   - **V2**: it lasts as long as the czar process stays hung. Nothing on the member side ends it: there is no deadline, the live kernel answers TCP keepalives, and `Halt` isn't checked. It ended only when the hung process was killed.
   - **V1**: it ends when the kernel's SYN retries run out. By then the harm the finding describes has already happened: about 135 s with no failover and no operating lease, instead of about 5 s.
   - **No masking**: nothing else filled czar-ship during the stall. Other members taking over later would not restore the stuck member's lease or let it shut down.

## Recommendation
- **Put a time limit on the czar dial in `czar.go:1382-1389`.** Set `ccfg.ConnectTimeout` well below the 5 s lease (for example ≤2 s). Call `StartWithCtx` with a timeout context instead of `Start()`, as commit 6afee204 did for the autoclient.
- **Make the rpc25519 dial respect that limit everywhere.**
  - `runClientMain` should also cancel a dial in progress when the client is closed, so that a cancelled `Start` doesn't leave a goroutine stuck in the TLS handshake.
  - `runClientTCP` (`cli.go:286`) calls `net.Dial` and ignores `ConnectTimeout` entirely. It should use `(&net.Dialer{Timeout: ...}).DialContext`.
  - Consider giving tube configs a finite default `ConnectTimeout`.
- **Add a regression test on real sockets** that checks takeover stays close to the lease duration against a dropped-packet czar and a stopped TLS czar, like V1 and V2 here.
- **A separate problem I noticed but didn't confirm.** The regular heartbeat `rpcClientToCzar.Call("Czar.Ping", ..., nil)` at `czar.go:1478` also has no deadline. It could stall members that are already connected to a dead or hung czar, and should get a timeout context too.

# CR-D-78: TubeNode.CAS panics on an already-cancelled context

CR-D-78 is reproduced at Level 0, using only the public API on a real 3-node cluster. In all four cancelled-context cases CAS panicked, and with nothing recovering it, the calling process died. The finding's claim that czar and hermes crash is not supported by the current code; that part is overstated.

- **Source**: Code Review
- **Novelty**: NEW. I searched the upstream glycerine/rpc25519 tracker through the GitHub API: there are 0 issues and 0 PRs in any state, and no search hits. The newest upstream commit to `tube/actions.go` (5c618571, 2026-10-17) is already in the tested tree. The Specular findings registry lookup returned nothing.
- **Severity**: Medium
- **Location**: `tube/actions.go:186` (request-ctx branch) and `tube/actions.go:191` (session-ctx branch), inside `TubeNode.CAS` at `tube/actions.go:183-194`

## Description
Both early-exit guards at the top of `TubeNode.CAS` call `panicf(...)` before their intended `err = ErrNeedNewSession; return`. `panicf` is just `panic(...)` (`tube/vprint.go:295-297`), so those return lines never run. A CAS called with an expired or cancelled ctx, on a closed session, or after the client node shut down panics. Nothing on the path recovers, so the whole process crashes.

The surrounding code returns an error in the same situations:
- `TubeNode.Write` returns `context deadline exceeded` for the same expired ctx.
- `Session.CAS(nil, …)` returns `ErrNeedNewSession` for the same closed session.
- CAS's own `select` returns `ctx.Err()` or `sess.ctx.Err()` when the cancel happens mid-call (`actions.go:256-262`, `282-288`).

## Trigger scenario
All three use only public calls:
1. **Expired or cancelled request ctx.** The caller's deadline passes, or shutdown cancels the ctx. Then `node.CAS(ctx, …, sess=nil, …)` panics at `:186`.
2. **Closed session.** `sess.Close()`, then `sess.CAS(context.Background(), …)`. This is exactly tup's call at `tube/cmd/tup/tup.go:468`. `Session.CAS` only checks the request ctx when it is non-nil (`:971-976`), never the session ctx, so the call reaches `:191` and panics.
3. **Client node shut down.** `TubeNode.Close()` cancels every session ctx, because sessions derive from `MyPeer.Ctx` (`tube.go:16126`, `:753`). The next `sess.CAS(Background, …)` panics at `:191`; `Session.Write` returns `error timeout` instead.

Which in-tree callers can reach it:
- **tup:** reachable. tup always passes `context.Background()`. Its `needNewSess` closes the session (`tup.go:151`). If re-creating it then fails with an error that doesn't contain "call CreateNewSession first" or "no leader known", it hands back the closed session (`tup.go:172`), and the next `cas` command crashes tup. I traced this from the code; I did not drive it end to end.
- **czar, hermes, member:** not reachable today. The czar (`czar.go:1037`, `:1300`) always passes a 5s ctx created on the line just before, and `sess=nil`. The session branch needs `czar.slow`, which is never set anywhere. The existing czar test Test808 passes with 0 panics (`repro/CR-D-78.czar808.log`).
- **Secondary path, not reproduced:** inside `Session.CAS`, ctx is checked at `:972`, then `prepareCommand` can spend up to 5s recovering an idle session before `:185` checks again. A deadline that expires in that gap would reach `:186` even through the wrapper.

## Developer intent
- `git log -L` on the site shows both guards were first added as `vv(...)` debug logs followed by `err = ErrNeedNewSession; return` (commits 78bd6109 and a3c0b4c7, with comments "seen a ton" and "firing _every_ time!").
- Commit 2b9ada4d, titled "atgs. but not good. fuzz_test 101 green …", then changed `vv(` to `panicf(` and left the return lines in place. Commit 55599962 added `sess != nil &&` to cover the czar's nil session.
- The developers' fuzz harness expects `ErrNeedNewSession` back from `Session.CAS` (`fuzz_test.go:1542`, `:1669`). No doc or test says CAS panics.

So the intended behaviour is the error return, and the panic looks like a leftover debugging tripwire.

## Reproduction result
Level 0: no failpoints, no state injection, no source change. The test is `repro/test_bugCR-D-78_cas_cancelled_ctx_panic_test.go`, run with `bash repro/test_bugCR-D-78_run.sh`. That copies the test into the worktree's `tube/`, runs `timeout 600 go test -tags synctest -count=1 -run … -v .`, and removes the copy afterwards. Output from `repro/CR-D-78.log`:
```
CRD78: cluster up: 3 nodes, leader=node_0
CRD78: C0 control: sess.CAS(live ctx) on live session                                 -> returned (no panic): err=<nil>
CRD78: S1 dctx.Err()=context deadline exceeded
CRD78: S1a sibling: TubeNode.Write(expired ctx, sess=nil)                             -> returned (no panic): err=context deadline exceeded
CRD78: S1b BUG?: TubeNode.CAS(expired ctx, sess=nil)  [czar call shape]               -> PANIC: crd78_client: TubeNode.CAS sees already cancelled ctx, bailing early
CRD78: S1c BUG?: TubeNode.CAS(cancelled ctx, live sess)                               -> PANIC: crd78_client: TubeNode.CAS sees already cancelled ctx, bailing early
CRD78: S1d guard: Session.CAS(expired ctx) [wrapper pre-checks ctx]                   -> returned (no panic): err=need new session
CRD78: S2 after sess.Close(): sess.ctx.Err()=context canceled
CRD78: S2a intended contract: Session.CAS(nil ctx) on closed session                  -> returned (no panic): err=need new session
CRD78: S2c BUG?: Session.CAS(Background) on closed session [tup call]                 -> PANIC: crd78_client: TubeNode.CAS sees already cancelled sess.ctx, bailing early
CRD78: S3 after cli2.Close(): sess2.ctx.Err()=context canceled
CRD78: S3a sibling: Session.Write(live ctx) after node shutdown                       -> returned (no panic): err=error timeout
CRD78: S3b BUG?: Session.CAS(Background) after node shutdown                          -> PANIC: crd78_client2: TubeNode.CAS sees already cancelled sess.ctx, bailing early
CRD78: SUMMARY: 4 of 4 cancelled-context CAS calls panicked instead of returning an error
--- PASS: TestBugCRD78_cas_cancelled_ctx_panics (0.38s)
```
The test PASSes when the bug is triggered. Running the same calls without `recover()` (`CRD78_CRASH=sess` and `=ctx`) kills the test process:
```
panic: crd78_crash_client: TubeNode.CAS sees already cancelled sess.ctx, bailing early [recovered, repanicked]
github.com/glycerine/rpc25519/tube.(*TubeNode).CAS(...)  .../tube/actions.go:191 +0xcf4
github.com/glycerine/rpc25519/tube.(*Session).CAS(...)   .../tube/actions.go:982 +0x22a
FAIL github.com/glycerine/rpc25519/tube 0.387s
panic: crd78_crash_client: TubeNode.CAS sees already cancelled ctx, bailing early [recovered, repanicked]
github.com/glycerine/rpc25519/tube.(*TubeNode).CAS(...)  .../tube/actions.go:186 +0xd65
```
- **Other runs:** the same 4/4 result appears in real time without synctest (`CR-D-78.realtime.log`, 5.0s) and on a scratch copy of the registry's source root (`CR-D-78.sourceroot.log`).
- **Fix control:** on that scratch copy I deleted only the two `panicf` lines (`CR-D-78.fixcontrol.patch`). All four cases then returned `need new session`, the test reported "CR-D-78 NOT reproduced", and the unrecovered run passed without crashing. This shows the two `panicf` lines are the whole cause.

**Checklist**
1. Level 0 or 1 alone? **Yes**, Level 0. Only public calls are used. The only timing is the caller's own deadline passing before the call, which is the trigger itself.
2. Not applicable. No state injection or source patch was used to trigger it. The source edit was only the fix control, on a scratch copy, and it removes the symptom.
3. Real caller: any caller of the exported API. In the runs, the calling process crashes with the stacks above. In-tree, `tube/cmd/tup/tup.go:468` makes exactly the S2c call. The way tup ends up holding a closed session (`tup.go:151` / `:172`) comes from reading the code, not from an end-to-end tup run. `czar.go:1037` and `:1300` (czar, hermes) do not reach it in the current code.
4. Permanent: **yes**. An unrecovered panic ends the process, and there is no `recover()` in the library, tup, czar or hermes paths. The `Session.CAS` wrapper only covers the request-ctx case for Session callers (S1d). It does not cover the session-ctx case (S2c, S3b) or direct `TubeNode.CAS` calls (S1b, S1c).

## Recommendation
- Delete the two `panicf` lines so the existing `return ErrNeedNewSession` runs. Returning `ctx.Err()` in the request-ctx branch would match Write and Read. This fix is the one validated above.
- In `Session.CAS`, also check `s.ctx.Err()` when `ctx != nil`, before calling `prepareCommand`.
- If a debugging tripwire is still wanted, make it a log line or a test-only assertion, not a production panic.
- Separately, tup's `needNewSess` should not return a session it has already closed.

The full write-up is in `confirmation/CR-D-78/confirmation.md`, with the evidence record in `investigation.md`. The persistent record is `confirmation/CR-D-78/issue.json`, and `specular findings … validate` reported it valid.

CR-D-79 is reproduced at Level 0, using the unmodified `tube`, `tubels`, `tubeadd` and `tup` binaries over real TLS. Every replica that received a message with another cluster's ClusterID crashed: the event loop panicked and the whole process exited with status 2. The correct behaviour would be to drop the message.

- **Source**: Code Review
- **Novelty**: NEW
- **Severity**: High
- **Location**: `tube/tube.go:1665`. Also the same panic-instead-of-drop at `tube/tube.go:1745, 1759, 1823, 1873, 1887, 1902, 1932, 1975, 1681, 2156` and the `panicOn` after each payload decode. The process dies because of the re-panic at `tube/tube.go:806-808` and the goroutine without a `recover` at `ckt.go:1661-1673`.
- **Reproduction test**: `.specular-output/repro/test_bugCR-D-79_wrong_cluster_crashes_replicas.sh`

## Description
Every frag a tube node builds (`newFrag`, `tube/tube.go:12687`) carries the sender's ClusterID. The replica event loop runs `notOurClusterAndNotCircuitStart` on each arriving frag, and that function correctly reports "drop" when the ClusterID differs. The caller then logs `dropping frag not in our cluster` and runs `panic("what? no cluster tests yet!")` before its `continue` (`tube/tube.go:1662-1666`). `TubeNode.Start`'s deferred `recover` tears the node down and panics again. The rpc25519 goroutine that runs `Start` has no `recover`, so the replica process exits. The same handler also panics on:
- a ClusterID mismatch inside the payload;
- an unknown FragOp;
- `NotifyClientNewLeader` arriving at a replica;
- an empty `RemotePeerName`;
- a payload that fails to unmarshal.

## Trigger scenario
I built a healthy 3-node cluster with ClusterID "123", following `tube/example/local/README.md`: shared `tube` cert from `selfy`, three `tube` processes, `tubeadd node_0/1/2`, then `tubels` and a `tup` write. Then:
- **A — stale client config:** `~/.config/tube/tup.default.config` says ClusterID "456" but lists the same nodes, and the operator runs `tubels`. `HelperFindLeader` (`tube/helper.go:104-134`) sends a `PeerListReq` to the nodes.
- **B — foreign replica:** a `tube` replica for cluster "456" whose `Node2Addr` also lists the cluster-123 addresses starts up. Its normal startup call to `HelperFindLeader` (`tube/tubecmd.go:184`) contacts those nodes.

## Developer intent
- The code shows the intent was to drop: the `alwaysPrintf("dropping frag …")` line, the dead `continue // drop` after each panic, and the "// drop or reply? probably drop." comment (`tube/tube.go:1874`). The function's own comment says it is "centralize rejecting … wrong cluster garbage".
- `LeaderToClientTicketAppliedMsg` already logs a wrong ClusterID and skips it (`tube/tube.go:1772-1775`).
- The panic text itself admits there are no tests, and none of the tests send a mismatched ClusterID. The code dates from the first import (`aa45ba104`, 2025-09-18).
- Prior-report search on 2026-11-23: `glycerine/rpc25519` has 0 issues and 0 PRs in any state, and a search for "ClusterID" in the repo returns nothing. Upstream `master` (`150bf57a`) and the `claude` and `specular` branches still contain all of these panics. So this is NEW.

## Reproduction result
Command: `timeout 15m bash repro/test_bugCR-D-79_wrong_cluster_crashes_replicas.sh <worktree> confirmation/CR-D-79/repro-evidence`. It exited 0, and the full log is in `confirmation/CR-D-79/repro-run.log`.

07:35:44 [repro] Scenario A (stale-config tubels): replicas reached by foreign frag=1, of those exited with panic=1
07:35:44 [repro] Scenario B (foreign replica)     : replicas reached by foreign frag=2, of those exited with panic=2
07:35:44 [repro] BUG REPRODUCED: every replica that received a foreign-ClusterID frag panicked in the event loop (tube/tube.go:1665, re-panicked by Start's defer at tube/tube.go:807) and its process exited, instead of dropping the frag.
```
- The lines that show the bug are `dropping frag not in our cluster`, `panic: what? no cluster tests yet! [recovered, repanicked]`, the stack pointing at `tube.go:1665` and `tube.go:807`, and `EXITED (status 2)`.
- As a control, every client using the correct ClusterID left all replicas running.
- An earlier run, which used a stricter "all 3 must die" check I then corrected, gave the same result: 1 of 1 reached replicas died in A, and 2 of 2 in B.
- Some panic sites were not exercised. I argue them from the code only:
  - The payload-level ClusterID panics are hit only after the frag-level check passes. A normal sender trips `1665` first.
  - Unknown FragOp needs a newer binary during a rolling upgrade.
  - `NotifyClientNewLeader` at a replica, empty `RemotePeerName`, and payload unmarshal errors.

## Recommendation
- Replace `panic` with log-and-drop (`continue`) at `1665` and at each payload-level ClusterID check.
- For an unknown FragOp or a payload that fails to unmarshal: log, drop, and optionally close that circuit.
- Ignore `NotifyClientNewLeader` at a non-client.
- Reject a circuit with an empty `RemotePeerName` instead of panicking.
- Optionally, check ClusterID when the circuit is set up.
- Add a regression test: a client with a different ClusterID runs `HelperFindLeader` against a simnet cluster, and every replica must stay up.

`issue.json` is written and passes `specular findings validate`. Phase 1 notes are in `confirmation/CR-D-79/investigation.md`.

## Checklist
1. **Level 0 or Level 1 alone?** Yes, Level 0 only. Stock binaries, a real cluster built with the documented steps, and the only change was a ClusterID in a config file. No timing help, no state injection, no source patch.
2. Not applicable, since no Level 2 or Level 3 was used.
3. **Who observes the wrong outcome?** The `tube` replica process itself. The path is `cmd/tube/tubecli.go` → `RunTubeServiceMain` (`tube/tubecmd.go:77`) → `TubeNode.Start` event loop (`tube/tube.go:1665`), and the process terminates with status 2. The cluster loses that member.
4. **Permanent?** Yes. The process stays dead: nothing in the repo supervises or restarts it, and no sync or resend mechanism resolves or masks the crash. An operator restart recovers the node from its on-disk state. I am not claiming any data loss.

# CR-D-80: a stale client URL dialed after a leader change panics the new leader

**Verdict: REPRODUCED.** The new leader crashed in 7 of 7 runs on the worktree (with a realistic timeline) and 3 of 3 on a copy of the current source. Both negative controls stayed clean.

- **Source**: Code Review
- **Novelty**: NEW. I searched the glycerine/rpc25519 tracker through the GitHub API: there are 0 issues and 0 PRs, open or closed, and keyword searches for this mechanism found nothing. The Specular case-studies tree has no tube or rpc25519 entry. Git history only has the developer's own debug commits about the symptom (73e3df0b, 3143c88b, b95ba711, a724f8d5). None of them identifies the mechanism.
- **Location**: tube/tube.go:9181 (HEAD `aae88ecf`). This is the `panic("fix this mis-directed fragment!")` inside `if true {` at :9172 in `peerJoin`. The stale dial is at tube/tube.go:7531, and the unconfirmed PeerID is set in ckt.go:553-616.

## Description
After a leader change, `notifyClientSessionsOfNewLeader()` (tube/tube.go:7482) dials the `ClientURL` stored in any session that has no live circuit under its client name.
- **The leader trusts the URL's PeerID.** `NewCircuitToPeerURL` copies that PeerID into `ckt.RemotePeerID` (ckt.go:600, :1126). The remote's acknowledgement is dropped, so the PeerID is never checked.
- **The client side creates a new identity.** If a different process now listens at that address, its rpc server finds no peer with the stale PeerID. Because `tube-client` has no service limit, it creates a new local peer with a fresh PeerID (ckt.go:1990, :2026). It also runs `TubeNode.Start` a second time on the client (ckt.go:1667), which overwrites the client's PeerID, URL and MyPeer.
- **The leader panics on the next frame.** The client's next frame on that circuit carries the new PeerID (ckt.go:712). The new leader's `peerJoin` sees a PeerID that differs from `ckt.RemotePeerID` and hits the debug panic that a724f8d5 switched back on. `Start`'s defer re-panics, so the leader process crashes right after it was elected.

## Trigger scenario
1. A 3-node cluster runs with leader node_0, over real TCP.
2. Client A listens on a fixed address `127.0.0.1:P` (PeerID P1), opens a session and writes. Every replica's session table now records A's URL with P1.
3. A exits without ending its session, as a crash, kill or restart would. The entry stays until it expires (default 10 minutes).
4. The restarted client B listens on the same address with PeerID P2. B may use a new random name, as `tup` and `member` clients do, or keep A's name if it has not opened a session yet.
5. node_0 crashes and node_1 or node_2 is elected. The new leader has no circuit to A, so it dials the stale URL. B's server creates a new peer (P3) and re-runs `B.Start`. B learns the new leader over that circuit.
6. B does ordinary work (`CreateNewSession`). Its request goes out as `RedirectTicketToLeader` from P3 over that same circuit.
7. The new leader's `peerJoin` sees P3 ≠ P1, panics, and the leader process dies.

## Developer intent
- **73e3df0b** (2026-01-14) pastes a production panic with the same shape as this reproduction:
  - the circuit is named `tube-ckt`, its first fragment is `NotifyClientNewLeader`, and it was opened by an auto-client (`MadeNewAutoCli: true`);
  - a `member_*` client sends `RedirectTicketToLeader` from a different PeerID at the same address;
  - the stack is the same: `peerJoin` ← `TubeNode.Start` ← `unlockedStartLocalPeer.func1`.
- **3143c88b** reports "mis-directed packet now reproducible" in fuzz test 101.
- **b95ba711** turned the check off ("Let's try not freaking out").
- **a724f8d5** ("wip debug mis-routed frag") turned it back on ("let's make sure!"). It is still on after 290 later commits.

So the developers saw the symptom but never found the cause. A `panic` that network input can reach, left on for debugging, is not intended production behaviour.

## Reproduction result
**Level 0.** The test uses only the public TubeNode API on real TCP, plus process exit and a leader crash as the operational events. There is no injected state, no simnet and no source change.

**Command:** `repro/test_bugCR-D-80_stale_client_url_leader_panic.sh 3`

- Line 89: the node that panics is the newly elected leader.
- Lines 114–154: the circuit is the one opened by the stale dial.
- Line 35: B's PeerID was replaced by a third ID.

**Expected behaviour**, shown by both controls (A ends its session first, or B uses another port): B keeps P2, all five of B's writes succeed, and the leader stays leader.

**Same defect in the current source.** I ran the same script against a copy of glycerine/rpc25519 at `f6da80e7`, which includes the later Bug 3–16 fixes. The four cited functions are byte-identical there. The result was 2/2 bug runs plus the same-name variant panicking, with both controls clean (`confirmation/CR-D-80/current-source-run/`).

**A second harmful outcome of the same stale dial.** In my first attempt the leader crashed right after A's last write, before every replica had applied it.
- The new leader's first frame to the stale PeerID was then unroutable, so B's server dropped the connection (srv.go:811).
- That ended the duplicate `B.Start` (tube/tube.go:2017), which halted all of client B. B's later calls failed with "halt requested".
- `f6da80e7` ("Fix Bug 9") now drops such frames instead of closing the connection. That route therefore now ends in the leader panic.
- The logs are in `confirmation/CR-D-80/diag-*.log`. The instrumented scratch copy only added print statements.

**Checklist:**
1. **Level 0 or 1 alone triggered it?** Yes. The only waits make the timeline realistic: replicas apply A's write before the crash, and B sits idle for 2 seconds.
2. **State injection or source patch?** Not used.
3. **Who sees the wrong outcome?** The new leader's `TubeNode.Start` event loop, which calls `s.peerJoin` at tube/tube.go:1668. It panics at :9181, and the process dies through the re-panic at :802-804. B's session request is lost, and B is left with a rewritten PeerID and a second event loop on the same node.
4. **Permanent or masked?** Permanent. It is a process crash, and no recover, sync or resend undoes it. The stale session stays in replicated state until it is ended or expires, and every later election repeats the dial. That it recurs on each new leader is argued, not demonstrated: in-process, the first panic ends the test binary.

## Recommendation
1. **Stop crashing the replica.** Remove the `if true { … panic }` block in `peerJoin`. On a mismatch, drop the frame and close or replace the circuit.
2. **Don't trust the PeerID in a stored URL.** In `notifyClientSessionsOfNewLeader`, either:
   - dial by address and service without a PeerID, and adopt the PeerID the remote acknowledges; or
   - wait for the acknowledgement and set `RemotePeerID` from it.

   The rpc layer already stamps `oldPeerID/newPeerID/newPeerURL` (ckt.go:2137-2139), but nothing reads them.
3. **Don't re-run the service on a live process for an unknown PeerID.** `bootstrapCircuit` should reject a dial to a PeerID it no longer hosts. At minimum, `TubeNode.Start` should refuse a second call, or `tube-client` should be capped at one instance through `LimitedServiceNames`.
4. **Decouple the new peer's lifetime from the connection.** A peer created for a remote request should not take the triggering connection's context as its parent (ckt.go:1640).

# CR-D-81: same-named replica processes both vote, so two leaders are elected in one term

- **Source**: Code Review
- **Novelty**: NEW
- **Location**: tube/tube.go:7259 (also tube/tube.go:7082-7102, tube/tube.go:16729-16880, ckt.go:2102-2107, hostkey.go:268-281)

## Description
Tube identifies a voter by the name the remote process writes in its own message headers. `provideRemoteOnNewCircuitCh` (ckt.go:2102-2107) copies `msg.HDR.FromPeerName` and `FromPeerID` straight into the remote-peer record. The TLS check (hostkey.go:268-281) only asks whether the key is one it already knows; it never ties the key to a name.

The finding says the sample configs use TCP without TLS; that is only half right. The per-node configs (`tube.N.cfg`) do use TLS, but every node uses the same `"tube"` keypair. The `tube.sample.cfg` templates and the tests use TCP-only. Either way, nothing distinguishes one node from another.

How votes are counted:
- Each voter grants at most one vote per term, from its own state on disk (`handleRequestVote`, tube.go:11504).
- Each candidate counts at most one vote per name (`tallyVote` 7257-7264, `tallyPreVote` 7095-7102), and quorum is a majority of the names in the membership config (6931-6958).
- When a second process claims an existing name, `addToCktall` (16729-16880) keeps both of its IDs in its circuit maps and the leader replicates to both.

So two processes started with the same name but separate state directories are two independent voters for one name. Two different candidates can each count a different copy, and both reach quorum.

## Trigger scenario
1. A cluster of `node_0`, `node_1` and `node_2` (call it X) is running, with node_0 leading term 3.
2. By mistake, a second process Y is started with `MyName: node_2` and its own default data directory. Y dials node_0 and node_1. The leader then tracks two peers named node_2 and replicates the log and membership config to Y.
3. All four processes crash, then restart from their own state directories. The link between the two racks stays down: rack 1 is {node_0, X}, rack 2 is {node_1, Y}.
4. Each rack holds 2 of the 3 names, so each rack elects a leader in term 4.
5. One client writes `k=client-A` through rack 1's leader and another writes `k=client-B` through rack 2's leader. Both writes are acknowledged as committed at the same position (index 6, term 4).
6. The link comes back. The two logs keep different entries at (6, 4). Raft's consistency check compares only index and term, so it never notices. One acknowledged write disappears, and a later leader change can bring it back.

## Developer intent
- The comment on the vote dedup in `tallyVote` (tube.go:7257) reads "dedup votes by Name not PeerID so even if they restart they don't get to vote twice!" Names are meant to be the voter identity and double voting is meant to be prevented. Only restarts that reuse the same state were considered.
- czar.go:997-1006 guards leases "if by mistake two members under the same name are started". The developer treats this mistake as plausible, but the Raft vote path has no equivalent guard.
- There is no data-directory lock. Unique names are documented and enforced only for the network simulator (simnet.go:1039, "server name already taken").
- Prior reports: the upstream repo has 0 issues and 0 PRs, open or closed. No commit and no earlier Specular record covers this. The repo now has fix commits for Bugs 5–16, newer than this worktree. None covers this mechanism. The closest, "Fix Bug 15: count a restarted replica once per quorum", changes how the leader counts acks, not how votes are granted. The reproduction still triggers on the latest HEAD (e36dfdac), 3 runs out of 3.

## Reproduction result
**How it was run:** Level 0. The test uses only the tube package's public calls and its standard test-cluster setup: `NewCluster`, `NewTubeNode`, `InitAndStart`, `Close`, `Write`, `Read`, `Inspect`. Nodes talk over real TCP, and each has its own state directory on disk. There are no failpoints, no source changes and no injected state; Y gets its log only through normal replication. The partition is modelled by not connecting the cross-rack links. The public `cfg.NoBackgroundConnect=true` setting stops nodes from reconnecting around it.

**Command:** `CRD81_RUNS=5 repro/test_bugCR-D-81_dupname_two_leaders.sh` (each run is a separate `go test`). The script copies the test file into the worktree and removes it afterwards; the worktree was verified clean.

**Control, no duplicate:**
```
CRD81: CONTROL: rack1 leaders=1 ; node_1 (alone in rack2) role=FOLLOWER
CRD81: CONTROL: exactly one leader (node_2); the 1-of-3-names side cannot elect
```
**Bug, run 1:**
```
CRD81: phase 2: leader node_0 tracks 2 distinct peers named node_2 in s.peers: [oC1exfHQ vYpEl83D]
CRD81: RESULT: ELECTION SAFETY VIOLATED: two leaders (node_0, node_1) in the same term 4
CRD81: RESULT: node_2(X) (peerID=ocHLGRuw) voted in term 4 for node_0
CRD81: RESULT: node_2(Y) (peerID=nLdwJH5f) voted in term 4 for node_1
CRD81: client Write(k="client-A-via-rack1") via node_0 -> OK (committed) LogIndex=6 Term=4
CRD81: client Write(k="client-B-via-rack2") via node_1 -> OK (committed) LogIndex=6 Term=4
CRD81: RESULT: STATE MACHINE SAFETY VIOLATED: two different entries committed at the same (index=6, term=4)
CRD81: RESULT: linearizable reads of the same key disagree at the same time: "client-A-via-rack1" vs "client-B-via-rack2"
CRD81: RESULT: after heal k="client-A-via-rack1": client B's acknowledged committed write was LOST
CRD81: RESULT: LOG MATCHING VIOLATED after heal: entry (index=6, term=4) differs across replicas: map[node_0:[node_0 node_2(X)] node_1:[node_1 node_2(Y)]]
CRD81: RESULT: new leader node_1 serves k="client-B-via-rack2" (was "client-A-via-rack1" before the crash; no client wrote k in between)
CRD81: RESULT: COMMITTED VALUE FLIPPED without any write: "client-A-via-rack1" -> "client-B-via-rack2"
```
**Summary of the final scripted run (exit 0):**
```
bug runs with two leaders in the SAME term:              5 / 5
bug runs with two concurrent leaders both committing:    5 / 5
REPRODUCED
```
- **Across every run on this machine:** two leaders in the same term in 18 of 19 runs. The other run had a split vote inside one rack, giving leaders in terms 4 and 5, and both still committed.
- **After the heal:** in one exploratory run both node_2 processes were still leaders of term 4 twenty seconds later.
- **Not used as evidence:** some exploratory runs stalled with no new leader after the post-heal leader crashed. In those runs the surviving processes had lost their links to each other, and the test cannot reconnect them, so the stall may come from the test setup.

**Expected (correct) behaviour:** as in the control, the rack without node_2 holds only 1 of 3 names and cannot elect. There is at most one leader per term, and no acknowledged write is lost.

## Recommendation
- **Persistent node identity:** on first start, store a random per-replica ID in the data directory and record name → ID in the membership config. Vote handling (`handleRequestVote`, `tallyVote`, `tallyPreVote`) and `addToCktall` should reject a peer whose ID doesn't match. Changing the ID should require an explicit membership change.
- **Per-node certificates:** check that the certificate's identity matches the claimed `PeerName`, and stop shipping a single shared `tube` keypair in the examples.
- **Duplicate detection:** treat a second live connection claiming the same name under a different ID as a fault, and refuse it rather than keeping both. Also lock the data directory.

## Pre-REPRODUCED checklist
1. Level 0 or 1 alone? **Yes.** Level 0: normal APIs plus crash, restart and a network split. No timing help was needed.
2. Not applicable; no state injection or source changes were used.
3. Real consumers seeing a wrong outcome: `TubeNode.Write` (tube/actions.go:95) acknowledges two conflicting writes as committed at the same (6, 4). `TubeNode.Read` (tube/actions.go:316) returns different values on the two leaders at the same moment. After the heal, one acknowledged write is gone, and a later leader change can flip the value back.
4. **Permanent:** the conflicting entries at (6, 4) survive the heal, and Raft's consistency check matches on index and term only, so it never repairs them. A leader that sees the other's same-term messages steps down (tube.go:8203-8216), but that only settles who leads; the conflicting committed entries remain. Nothing masks the harm.

Files are in `.specular-output`:
- `repro/test_bugCR-D-81_dupname_two_leaders.sh`, `repro/test_bugCR-D-81_dupname_two_leaders_test.go`, and their output (`.out`, `.control.log`, `.bug.run1-5.log`)
- `confirmation/CR-D-81/investigation.md`, `confirmation/CR-D-81/confirmation.md`
- `confirmation/CR-D-81/issue.json`, which passes `specular findings validate`
- `confirmation/CR-D-81/head-e36dfdac-run/` (latest-HEAD rerun), `confirmation/CR-D-81/exploratory-runs/`

- **Source**: Code Review
- **Novelty**: NEW
- **Severity**: n/a (not a defect; the finding proposed Medium)
- **Location**: tube/tube.go:12707 (`insaneTooOldOrNew`; the finding cites 12624-12642, but lines have drifted), call site tube/tube.go:1656
- **Reproduction test**: `repro/test_bugCR-D-82_clock_skew_deafness.sh` (Level 0). Output in `repro/CR-D-82.log`; per-node logs in `repro/CR-D-82.run/`.

## Description
The core mechanism is real: two nodes whose clocks differ by more than 10 minutes can't talk to each other at all. `insaneTooOldOrNew` (tube/tube.go:12707-12725) runs on every incoming fragment at the top of the main loop (tube.go:1656-1661). It drops any fragment whose `frag.Created` is more than 10 minutes away from the receiver's `time.Now()`. `Created` is the sender's wall clock at send time (ckt.go:878, carried through ckt.go:851).

The finding's two extra claims are wrong:
- **The drops are not silent.** Every drop is logged with `alwaysPrintf`: 199 and 178 lines on the skewed node, plus 21–96 lines on its peers.
- **The skewed leader does step down.** It never sees the higher term, but it steps down through the Raft §6.2 check-quorum timer (tube.go:1455-1558) about 6.4 s after the clock jump.

The isolation itself is documented, intended behaviour. It fences off a node whose clock is far outside the system's own declared bound: `ClockDriftBound` defaults to 500 ms, and production config refuses values above 60 s (admin.go:471-473). The cluster treats that node like a minority partition. The correctly-clocked majority keeps electing leaders and committing writes, and the node recovers by itself once its clock is fixed. No client sees a wrong result, and no Raft invariant or majority-liveness guarantee is broken.

## Trigger scenario
Each scenario uses a fresh 3-node cluster: separate `tube` processes over loopback TCP with on-disk logs, driven through the public client API (`AddPeerIDToCluster`, `CreateNewSession`, `Session.Write`/`Read`).
- **S1 (follower):** node_2's host clock jumps +900 s and is held for about 39 s, then fixed. node_2 drops everything as "too old", and its peers drop its traffic as "too new". node_0 stays leader at term 1 and keeps committing. After the fix, node_2 rejoins and catches up with no restart.
- **S2 (leader):** leader node_0's clock jumps +900 s. It stays LEADER for about 6 s without being able to commit, then steps down while still at term 1. node_1 is elected at term 2 and commits and reads writes. After the fix, node_0 adopts term 2 and catches up.
- **S3 (control):** no skew. The leader is killed with SIGKILL and later restarted.

## Developer intent
- The function's doc comment has been there since tube was first imported (commit aa45ba10, 2025-09-18): *"Note this will also disable/deafen a node whose clock is massively wrong, on either sender or reader side."* The window was deliberately widened to 10 minutes; an in-code comment says the narrower window "discards legit traffic in 050 safety_test".
- `ClockDriftBound` (500 ms default, 60 s maximum) is the inter-node clock-disagreement bound used by leases (actions.go:576,784,804; czar.go:1511). A skew over 10 minutes is at least 10 times that maximum.
- `fuzz_CLOCK_SKEW` is listed as a fuzz fault but not implemented (fuzz_test.go:290,2023), and no test exercises this filter.
- Prior-report search:
  - **Upstream tracker:** glycerine/rpc25519 has 0 issues and 0 PRs, open or closed.
  - **Recent commits:** none on any ref, including the "Fix Bug 1..7" commits, change this function.
  - **Persistent-findings lookup:** returned nothing.

  So this finding is NEW and is not dropped as already known.

## Reproduction result
**Level 0:** the real, unmodified Tube server and client API, real TCP and disks, no failpoints, and no edits to Tube or rpc25519. Only the environment fault is emulated. Linux time namespaces can't skew the wall clock per process, and libfaketime doesn't affect Go. So the binaries are built with `go build -overlay` replacing the standard library's `time.go`: `Now()` adds an offset read from a file every 200 ms, and the monotonic clock is untouched.

Command: `timeout 20m bash repro/test_bugCR-D-82_clock_skew_deafness.sh > repro/CR-D-82.log 2>&1`. I ran it twice and both runs passed 8 of 8 checks. Verbatim excerpt from the second run, long lines trimmed:
```

[08:07:13.597 real] node_2 wall clock stepped +900s

INSPECT 08:07:32.098Z responder=node_2 NO_RESPONSE (contact attempt timed out / no reply)
from node_2's own host: INSPECTONE 08:22:32.121Z responder=node_2 role=FOLLOWER believesLeader='' leaderTerm=1 lastLogTerm=1 lastLogIndex=3 ...
[08:07:52.193 real] drop log lines: node_2 'too old'=199 ; node_0 'too new'=23 ; node_1 'too new'=21
sample node_2 drop line : tube.go:1658 [goID 83] 2026-11-23T08:22:13.980092958+00:00 dropping frag outside our window: frag too old(now=2026-11-23 08:22:13.979943945 +0000 UTC m=+6.038586044): &rpc25519.Fragment{

t+  0.5s INSPECTONE 08:23:07.072Z responder=node_0 role=LEADER believesLeader='node_0' leaderTerm=1 lastLogTerm=1 lastLogIndex=3 ...
t+  5.6s INSPECTONE 08:23:12.176Z responder=node_0 role=LEADER believesLeader='node_0' leaderTerm=1 lastLogTerm=1 lastLogIndex=3 ...
t+  6.4s INSPECTONE 08:23:12.906Z responder=node_0 role=FOLLOWER believesLeader='' leaderTerm=1 lastLogTerm=1 lastLogIndex=3 lastLeaderActiveStepDown=08:23:12.855Z ...
INSPECT 08:08:22.344Z responder=node_1 role=LEADER believesLeader='node_1' leaderTerm=2 lastLogTerm=2 lastLogIndex=4 ...

CHECK S2.C1 PASS: skewed node_0 is deaf both ways: NO_RESPONSE to a correctly-clocked client, 178 'too old' drops logged; node_1/node_2 logged 96 'too new' drops
CHECK S2.C4 PASS: majority elected node_1 at term 2 and committed and read back a client write while the old leader was skewed

The step-down could only have come from §6.2: every other step-down path (tube.go:7293, 9953, 11276) needs incoming messages, which the leader wasn't receiving. The 5.3–6.4 s delay matches the configured follower-down window of 4×1.2 s + 0.5 s.

Checklist answers:
1. **Level 0/1 alone?** Yes, Level 0 triggered the isolation.
2. **State injection or patch?** Not applicable.
3. **Consumer seeing a wrong outcome?** None from this filter. Correctly-clocked clients fail over and commit. Only a client on the skewed host fails ("no leader reachable"), exactly as it would under a network partition.
4. **Permanent or masked?** Neither. The node recovers on its own once its clock is fixed, and §6.2 prevents a stuck leader by design rather than hiding a defect.

## Recommendation
No correctness fix is needed for this finding. Optional hardening:
- Document the clock-sync requirement (NTP within `ClockDriftBound`) in tube/README.md.
- Replace the flood of full-fragment log dumps with a rate-limited "peer X clock offset ≈ +15m" error or metric.
- Consider deriving the 10-minute window from config. As a design note (not claimed here), skews between `ClockDriftBound` and 10 minutes aren't fenced at all.

**A separate, real defect showed up during reproduction. It is not this finding and needs its own triage.**
- **Mechanism:** once a node whose clock ran fast is corrected, its far-future hybrid logical clock (HLC) spreads to every peer, because remote HLC merges are unbounded (tube/hlc.go:221-257). Session cleanup compares that HLC (tube.go:16364-16377) against session end times based on the local clock (tube.go:16280-16282). Every new client session is therefore deleted the moment it's created.
- **Effect:** the whole cluster rejects client operations with "unknown Ticket.SessionID" for roughly (skew − 10 min), including on leaders whose clocks were never wrong.
- **Evidence:**
  - **S4 timing probe:** with a +660 s skew, the first successful write came 59.3 s after the fix, against a prediction of 60 s.
  - **S3 control:** with no skew, crashing the leader and restarting it caused no failures.
- **Not covered by Bug 6:** commit 3777b44e ("Fix Bug 6") changes the apply loop but not the remote merge, so this likely survives it (not verified).
- **Write-up:** `confirmation/CR-D-82/separate-observation-HLC-session.md`.

No `issue.json` was written because false positives aren't persisted, and no repair request applies to a code-review finding.

# Confirmation Verdict — CR-D-83

- **Source**: Code Review (no MC counterexample; Scenario S12 robustness, reported by code review)
- **Novelty**: NEW (persistent-findings `lookup` → `[]`; git history shows the *client* read loop gained a `recover()` in `57ac7641`/`4ab597aa` but no issue/PR/commit reports the *server* read-loop crash on peer-controlled `magic7`; developer-authored `panic` + commented-out algorithm cases are not a filed report of this defect)
- **Location**: `compress.go:253` (panic) reached from `srv.go:669` → read loop with no recover (defer at `srv.go:629-636`); same mechanism at `chacha.go:632`, `common.go:290`, `ckt.go:2509`, `ckt.go:2533`, `ckt.go:1967`
- **Severity**: Medium (remote single-message node crash / DoS; escalates toward High for `TCPonly_no_TLS` clusters where it is unauthenticated and can be repeated against a Raft majority → cluster liveness loss)
- **Reproduction test**: `.specular-output/repro/test_bugCR-D-83_decompress_panic.sh` — executed, Level 0

## Description
The server read-loop goroutine `rwPair.runReadLoop` (`srv.go:619`, launched bare at `srv.go:403`) has **no `recover()`** in its defer (`srv.go:629-636`), unlike the client read loop (`cli.go:362`). On the unencrypted path it calls `workspace.readMessage` → `decomp.handleDecompress` (`compress.go:225`), which validates only the 7 fixed public magic bytes and then switches on the attacker-controlled 8th byte (`magic7`). Values `2,3,4,5,6` (which `decodeMagic7` still calls *valid* algorithms — lz4/zstd — but `handleDecompress` no longer implements) and any value `≥8` fall through to `default: panic("unknown magic7 …")` (`compress.go:253`). The panic unwinds to the top of the read-loop goroutine and **aborts the entire server process**. The same unrecovered-panic exposure exists at the other cited sites (ack-channel overflow `ckt.go:2509/2533`; duplicate peer instance `ckt.go:1967`; encrypted-path decompress `chacha.go:632`), all reached synchronously on the same no-recover goroutine.

## Trigger scenario
1. A server runs with a normal supported config `TCPonly_no_TLS = true` (used throughout the test suite, e.g. `ckt_test.go:45`). With `TCPonly_no_TLS`, `serveConn` (`srv.go:356`) skips the handshake block (which needs `!TCPonly_no_TLS && encryptPSK`) and the blabber is built with `encrypt=false`, so a raw peer reaches `common.go:readMessage` directly — no authentication.
2. A peer (adversarial, or merely a buggy/mis-configured client that set `CompressAlgo:"lz4"`) opens a plain TCP connection and sends one correctly-framed message: 7 fixed magic bytes `b3 5d 18 39 ac 8e 1d` + compression byte `0x02` + 8-byte big-endian length + body. These bytes pass the server's only wire validation (the 7-byte magic check).
3. The server read loop runs `handleDecompress(2, …)` → `default: panic` → process abort. One packet, whole node down. Repeating it against a Raft majority removes the quorum.

## Developer intent
Comments show the design assumed a *cooperating* peer set with symmetric compression settings (`cli.go:1166-1174`: "CompressionOff must be universal … we will panic"; the reader-makes-right notes in `common.go`). There is no promise of robustness to arbitrary peer input, and no test asserts the server survives a bad `magic7`. The client read loop was deliberately given a `recover()` (`cli.go:362`; commits `57ac7641`, `4ab597aa`) while the server loop was left unprotected — an asymmetry with no commentary. This is evidence the crash is an unintended gap, not an accepted trade-off: a reachable peer-triggered panic with a real consequence (node death) is a bug regardless of the cooperating-peer assumption.

## Reproduction result
Level 0, pure black box — real public server API (`NewConfig`/`NewServer`/`Start`) + a raw `net.Dial` peer. Command: `bash repro/test_bugCR-D-83_decompress_panic.sh`. Actual output:

```
##### CONTROL: benign compression byte (magic7=0) #####
server up at 127.0.0.1:40817 (mode=control)
sent framed message: magic7=0 bodyLen=16
CONTROL_OK: server still accepting connections after benign magic7=0 frame
---- go run exit code (mode=control): 0 ----

##### ATTACK: peer-controlled compression byte (magic7=2, lz4/unimplemented) #####
server up at 127.0.0.1:35333 (mode=attack)
sent framed message: magic7=2 bodyLen=16
panic: unknown magic7 '2'

goroutine 19 [running]:
github.com/glycerine/rpc25519.(*decomp).handleDecompress(...)
 .../worktree/compress.go:253 +0x214
github.com/glycerine/rpc25519.(*workspace).readMessage(0x1cca0f29a1a0, ...)
 .../worktree/common.go:307 +0x41f
github.com/glycerine/rpc25519.(*blabber).readMessage(...)
 .../worktree/chacha.go:296 +0x45
github.com/glycerine/rpc25519.(*rwPair).runReadLoop(0x1cca0f414708, ...)
 .../worktree/srv.go:669 +0x3b1
created by github.com/glycerine/rpc25519.(*Server).serveConn in goroutine 8
 .../worktree/srv.go:403 +0x38f
exit status 2

===================== VERDICT =====================
control: PASS (server survived benign magic7=0)
attack:  PASS (server read loop PANICKED with no recover; process aborted)

RESULT: REPRODUCED
```

The control (byte-identical valid message, only `magic7` differs) leaves the server up; flipping that one peer-controlled byte to `2` crashes the whole process with `exit status 2`. The stack is exactly the finding's path (`compress.go:253` ← `runReadLoop` `srv.go:669` ← `serveConn` `srv.go:403`) with **no recover frame**.

### Pre-REPRODUCED checklist
1. **Level 0 / Level 1 alone?** — **YES.** Level 0: public server API + a raw TCP socket (what any network peer is), no failpoints, no state injection, no source patch.
2. **Level 2/3 pre-condition reachability** — N/A (not used).
3. **Real consumer observing the wrong outcome** — the **server process itself**: `rwPair.runReadLoop` (`srv.go:669`) panics with no recover → `exit status 2`. In a Tube/Raft deployment this is the node process; crashing it drops all its client connections and removes it from the cluster.
4. **Permanent, or masked/resolved downstream?** — **Permanent.** The process is dead. No recover exists on the read-loop path (grep-confirmed and confirmed by the absence of any recover frame in the crash stack); no sync/resend/guard can un-crash the process. Not masked.

## Recommendation
Two independent fixes (apply both — defense in depth):
1. **Make decompression/compression total, not panicking.** In `handleDecompress` (`compress.go:253`) and `handleCompress` (`compress.go:239-241`), return an `error` for an unknown/unimplemented `magic7` instead of `panic`. The read loop already converts a `readMessage` error into "drop this one connection" (`srv.go:683-722`), so a bad peer would cost one connection, not the node.
2. **Add a `recover()` to the server read loop**, mirroring the client (`cli.go:362`): wrap `runReadLoop`'s defer (`srv.go:629`) so any panic in message handling (including the ack-overflow `ckt.go:2509/2533` and duplicate-peer `ckt.go:1967` sites, and the encrypted-path nil-decomp `chacha.go:632`) tears down only that connection rather than the process. Also consider demoting the `ckt.go` "out of space"/"more than 1 peer" panics to error returns, since they too are reachable from peer-driven input.

**Persistent record:** `issue.json` is intentionally omitted — a validate-passing one is not expressible under this run's registry (it requires a `root: source` dependency and rejects `..`, but the declared `source` is the `tube/` subdir while the affected code is the parent `rpc25519` package; `root: source` + `compress.go` binds to the wrong `tube/compress.go`). The finding is fully documented in `confirmation/CR-D-83/investigation.md` + the executed repro and its captured output above.

- **Source**: Code Review
- **Novelty**: NEW
- **Location**: tube/tube.go:14769 (`TubeNode.changeMembership`, at worktree HEAD c65ddda7). This is the line the finding cites as 14576-14581; on master 150bf57a it is at 14580, and at the newest pipeline commit e36dfdac it is at 14821.

CR-D-84 is a real bug and I reproduced it. A stale PeerID for a restarted node crashes the leader process, through the public API (Level 0) and also through the node's own self-add (Level 1).

## Description
An add-member ticket can carry a target PeerID (`tkt.AddPeerID`). When that value is non-empty and differs from the PeerID on the leader's live circuit to the same node name (`cktAllByName[name].PeerID`), `changeMembership` panics with "difference in opinion about peerID … is one of them stale?" (tube/tube.go:14768-14769).

The panic happens on the leader's event-loop goroutine:
- `TubeNode.Start`'s deferred `recover()` cleans up and then re-panics (tube/tube.go:806-808).
- `Start` runs in a bare goroutine with no recover (ckt.go:1691-1697).
- So the whole leader process exits.

A PeerID changes every time a node restarts, so any add request carrying a restarted node's old PeerID kills the leader. Commit 474ffe12 only exempted an empty live PeerID; this non-empty case still panics on every branch. The check is reached when the target is not currently a member (a new, removed or shadow node) and the leader has a live circuit to it.

## Trigger scenario
- **T1 (Level 0, public API):**
  1. Replica node_3 is up and connected to the leader, but not a member.
  2. An admin tool records node_3's PeerID P1.
  3. node_3 crashes and restarts with a new PeerID P2 and reconnects. `addToCktall` (tube/tube.go:17043-17051) then records P2 for node_3 on the leader.
  4. The tool calls `AddPeerIDToCluster(…, "node_3", P1, …)` from a separate client node, like cmd/tubeadd.
  5. On the leader, `RedirectTicketToLeaderMsg` (1871) → `commandSpecificLocalActionsThenReplicateTicket` (17456) → `changeMembership` → panic.
- **T2 (Level 1, no caller ever holds a stale value):**
  1. The operator replaces node_2 with node_3: remove node_2, so the new config is {node_0, node_1}.
  2. node_1's outbound sends are dropped for about 0.4s, a transient one-way network fault. The leader does not step down.
  3. node_3 adds itself with its own current PeerID, exactly as `tube -add` does (tubecmd.go:246).
  4. The leader stalls that add, because node_1 has not yet acknowledged the new config (Q1 check unmet). The stalled ticket keeps PeerID P1.
  5. node_3 restarts and reconnects with P2.
  6. The leader re-runs stalled membership tickets on every AppendEntries ack (tube.go:9938-9943). The next ack replays the stale ticket and the leader panics. node_3's own startup re-add would trigger the same replay.

## Developer intent
- The developers consistently treat the PeerID as ephemeral contact information and the node name as its identity:
  - `changeMembership`'s own rule comment (14605-14612): the details of how to reach a name "are fluid … as circuits die and are re-established".
  - "allow without PeerID -- only the name matters" (13401).
  - "how should we treat the PeerID? ephemeral? yes." (membership_test.go:48).
  - `parReconfigurationReady` quietly skips a PeerID from an old incarnation (par.go:2165-2167).
  - Unmerged review-branch commit 36d26a8d says the PeerID "is expected to change on restart".
- The panic's own text asks "is one of them stale?", and 474ffe12 relaxed a related case as a "spurious assert". Crashing the leader on an expected condition is a defect.
- **Prior reports:**
  - Upstream glycerine/rpc25519 has 0 issues and 0 PRs, and GitHub search found nothing.
  - In git history the panic text appears only in its introducing commit, aa45ba10. No branch or recent pipeline commit (f6da80e7…e36dfdac) changes it.
  - The persistent-findings registry lookup returned nothing.

## Reproduction result
Command: `repro/test_bugCR-D-84_stale_peerid.sh`. It runs `CRD84_REPEAT=3 go test -tags synctest -count=1 -run '^TestCRD84_reproduce$' -v` and re-runs the test binary once per scenario so it can detect the crash. Excerpt from `repro/CR-D-84.log`:
```
14769:     panic(fmt.Sprintf("difference in opinion about peerID for '%v'; which is correct? ...
  [stale_tool] CRD84: STALE_ID=SRd4LM2Ie2oCpnUOeJh5dVFGK7X6 (node_3 incarnation #1 PeerID, recorded by the admin tool)
  [stale_tool] CRD84: LIVE_ID=CQ8dpdEfW1Oz28Eigj4FihEaSWoJ (node_3 restarted: incarnation #2 PeerID)
  [stale_tool] CRD84: admin tool calls AddPeerIDToCluster(targetPeerName='node_3', targetPeerID='SRd4LM2Ie2oCpnUOeJh5dVFGK7X6', leaderURL=<node_0>)
  [stale_tool] panic: difference in opinion about peerID for 'node_3'; which is correct? cktP.PeerID='CQ8dpdEfW1Oz28Eigj4FihEaSWoJ', but tkt.AddPeerID = 'SRd4LM2Ie2oCpnUOeJh5dVFGK7X6'. is one of them stale? [recovered, repanicked]

Crash stack (`repro/CR-D-84.stale_selfadd.child.log`, abridged): `Start.func1 tube.go:807` ← `changeMembership tube.go:14769` ← `handleAppendEntriesAck tube.go:9942` ← `Start tube.go:1946` ← `unlockedStartLocalPeer.func1 ckt.go:1697`. The tool scenario reaches the panic through `commandSpecificLocalActionsThenReplicateTicket tube.go:17456` ← `Start tube.go:1871`.

- **Expected behaviour**, shown by the controls: an add with the current PeerID, an empty PeerID, or a stall without a restart all complete, and the leader stays up.
- **Newest source:** I also reproduced it at e36dfdac, the newest pipeline source (`repro/CR-D-84.e36dfdac.log`).
- **No-fault variant:** without the network fault, the self-add variant did not trigger in 3/3 runs, because the stall cleared before the restart finished (`CR-D-84.L0-selfadd-nofault.log`).

## Recommendation
Never panic on this mismatch. Let the live circuit's PeerID win, which is what already happens when the ticket's PeerID is empty, and log the stale value:
```go
peerID := cktP.PeerID // live incarnation wins; names are the identity
if peerID == "" { peerID = tkt.AddPeerID } else if tkt.AddPeerID != "" && tkt.AddPeerID != cktP.PeerID {
    alwaysPrintf("%v changeMembership: ignoring stale AddPeerID '%v' for '%v'; live PeerID '%v'", s.me(), tkt.AddPeerID, tkt.AddPeerName, cktP.PeerID)
}
```
If you'd rather be strict, fail just that ticket (`tkt.Err = …; s.replyToForwardedTicketWithError(tkt); return`) and keep the leader running. More broadly, treat fields of remote or forwarded tickets as untrusted input: because `Start` re-panics, any assert that client input can reach is a process crash. The stale_tool and stale_selfadd scenarios can be added as regression tests.

One risk I argued but did not demonstrate: if the stale request is retried, each new leader with a live circuit to the restarted node could crash in turn.

**Checklist**
1. Did Level 0 or Level 1 alone trigger it? **Yes.** stale_tool is Level 0: public `AddPeerIDToCluster` plus a normal crash/restart, with no faults, no state injection and no source changes. stale_selfadd is Level 1: it adds only the simulator's `DropSends` fault hook, about 0.4s on node_1.
2. Not applicable: no Level 2 or Level 3 was used.
3. The real consumer that sees the wrong outcome is the leader's event loop, `TubeNode.Start`. The panic reaches it through tube/tube.go:1871 → 17456 → 14769 in the tool case, and 1946 → 9942 → 14769 in the self-add case. It re-panics at tube/tube.go:807, the leader process exits (status 2), and the requester never gets an answer.
4. Permanent: the leader process is gone, and nothing in it recovers. Raft electing a new leader afterwards shortens the outage but does not undo the crash, so this is not MASKED.

Files are in `.specular-output`:
- `confirmation/CR-D-84/`: `investigation.md`, `report.md`, and `issue.json` (validated)

# CR-D-85: QUIC client never sets `c.cpair`, so keepalive and `PingStats` dereference nil, and a keepalive write timeout leaves a partial frame

All three parts of the finding reproduced through rpc25519's public API, with no rpc25519 source changes. (a) and (b) reproduce every time. (c) left a truncated frame in 11 of 16 attempts, and each truncation ended in a torn-down connection and a failed call. For Tube it only applies with non-default config (QUIC or keepalives turned on).

- **Source**: Code Review
- **Novelty**: NEW
- **Location**: quic_client.go:204

## Description
`runQUIC` creates `cpair := &cliPairState{}` and passes it to the send and read loops (quic_client.go:204-206), but never sets `c.cpair`. The TLS (cli.go:278), TCP (cli.go:337) and simnet (simnet_client.go:94) paths all set it.

Two places read the field rather than the parameter:
* the keepalive success branch of `runSendLoop`: `c.cpair.lastPingSentTmu.Store(...)` at cli.go:680 (upstream cli.go:671);
* the public `Client.PingStats`, at cli.go:2498 (upstream 2489).

The worktree's line numbers are 9 higher than upstream because of the Specular fix commits; the code is identical.

On a QUIC client this causes two failures:
* **(a)** The first successful keepalive panics. `runSendLoop`'s `recover()` then halts the whole Client and all of its circuits, permanently.
* **(b)** `PingStats` crashes the calling process.

**(c)** Separately, keepalives are the only frames written with a deadline (2 s). `sendMessage` writes each frame as three separate `writeFull` calls (common.go:374-385). `writeFull` (common.go:436-507) gives up after one 100 ms retry and returns, with part of the frame already written. The client only logs the error (cli.go:677-678) and keeps writing on the same connection, so the receiver misreads everything that follows.

## Trigger scenario
* **(a)** Set `UseQUIC=true` and `ClientSendKeepAlive=300ms`. Connect, make one call (it succeeds), then idle for 1.5 s. The keepalive goes out, the nil dereference fires, the client halts, and the next `SendAndGetReply` returns `shutting down`.
* **(b)** On any connected QUIC client, call `cli.PingStats(addr)`: the process dies with SIGSEGV, exit status 2.
* **(c)**
  1. Set up a TCP-only client with `ClientSendKeepAlive=5ms`, talking to the server through a proxy that stops reading client→server. This models a stalled receiver or a one-way network stall.
  2. During the stall, the app writes a burst of ordinary `OneWaySend` messages into the socket, up to just below the 4 MiB send buffer, then goes idle.
  3. Keepalives fill the rest of the buffer. The one whose 2 s deadline fires part-way through its frame is left truncated on the wire.
  4. When the path heals, the server's read loop hits a decode error and closes the connection (srv.go:718-722). The caller's next call fails.
* **Tube:** Tube's config file includes the full `RpcCfg`, so `UseQUIC` and `ClientSendKeepAlive` can be set there (tube/admin_test.go:86-111, tube/admin.go:51). The defaults leave both off (tube.go:2663-2688).

## Developer intent
* Commit 4ab597aa, "fix crash when keepalives are on as in goq", added `c.cpair = cpair // otherwise segfault when keepalive pings are on.` to the TLS path only. That is this same crash, fixed at one of the three places that needed it.
* Commits 6554d557 ("…KeepAlive over both quic and tcp available") and 630bac25, plus the comment at quic_client.go:106-109, show that app-level keepalives exist mainly because QUIC's own keepalives are unreliable.
* The `writeFull` comment (common.go:465-485) says "write deadlines … can corrupt the wire. But: Pings still use write timeouts… we try hard here not to send a half message". The single retry doesn't cover the gap between the three writes, or a retry that also times out.
* `Test031_PingStats` is disabled and only covers TCP. No test covers QUIC with keepalives, or `PingStats` on QUIC.
* Prior reports: upstream glycerine/rpc25519 has 0 issues and 0 PRs in any state (GitHub API, 2026-11-23). Searches for cpair, PingStats, keepalive, quic and "nil pointer" return nothing. Upstream master still lacks the assignment.

## Reproduction result
I ran `repro/test_bugCR-D-85_quic_nil_cpair.sh`. It copies `test_bugCR-D-85_quic_nil_cpair_test.go` and `test_bugCR-D-85_keepalive_partial_frame_test.go` into the module root and runs `go test -count=1 -v -run '^TestCRD85' .` under `timeout 15m`. Two full runs both exited 0 (`repro/CR-D-85.log`, `repro/CR-D-85.repeat2.log`).
